summary: OpenPGP is a message format for email and file encryption, but it lacks a standard, secure way to look up someone's public key. This experimental document specifies a DANE method that publishes OpenPGP public keys in DNS, so that a key can be located and checked using the DNSSEC-protected domain name system.

plainLanguage.summary: To send someone a locked message you need their padlock. This lets people put their padlock on a trusted public noticeboard, the domain name system, so anyone can find the right one.

questions: how to publish openpgp keys in dns
subtitle: Publish OpenPGP public keys in DNS for automatic email encryption.

tldr.problem: People who want to send encrypted email need the recipient's OpenPGP public key, but centralized keyservers are insecure: they do not verify email addresses, allow fake keys to be uploaded, and provide no way to revoke lost keys.
tldr.mechanism: The OPENPGPKEY DNS record type lets people publish their OpenPGP public key in their email domain's DNS zone, secured by DNSSEC. Email clients and servers can look up the key automatically and verify it came from the domain owner.
tldr.outcome: Email clients can now automatically find and encrypt to the right key without relying on untrustworthy centralized servers. This experiment is Experimental status and may not scale to large deployments.

today: RFC 7929 is an Experimental specification published in August 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated. Deployment remains limited, with some mail providers and clients supporting OPENPGPKEY lookups, but it has not achieved widespread adoption.

sections.title: The Problem with Keyservers
sections.content:
OpenPGP lets people encrypt email and files so only the intended recipient can read them. To encrypt a message to someone, you need their public key. The traditional way to find a public key is to ask a centralized keyserver over the HTTP Keyserver Protocol (HKP).

This approach has serious security problems. Keyservers do not verify that an uploaded key actually belongs to the email address listed on it. Attackers have uploaded fake keys with other people's email addresses. Once uploaded, keys cannot be deleted—even if the owner lost their private key and cannot create a revocation. This means someone might receive encrypted email they can never decrypt.

This document specifies a better way: publish OpenPGP keys in DNS, the system that translates domain names to addresses. DNS can be secured with DNSSEC so that keys are authenticated by the domain owner, not by an untrustworthy keyserver.
sections.plainLanguage: Keyservers are like a bulletin board anyone can pin notes to, and you cannot take your notes down. OPENPGPKEY puts your key in your own domain, which only you can update.

sections.title: The OPENPGPKEY Record
sections.content:
The OPENPGPKEY DNS record type (RR type 61) stores a single OpenPGP Transferable Public Key in DNS. The key is the binary OpenPGP format specified in RFC 4880, encoded in base64 for display.

To keep DNS records as small as possible, the key should be filtered before publishing. It should include the primary key, at least one User ID matching the email address, a self-signature binding the key to the email address, and if the primary key cannot encrypt, an encryption-capable subkey. Optional third-party certifications from the "web of trust" can be included to help recipients trust the key.

A person who wants to publish more than one key (for example, when transitioning to a stronger key) can publish multiple OPENPGPKEY records for the same email address. Each record contains exactly one key.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds your encrypted key in base64, the same format used in email. It should be as small as possible, keeping only the parts someone needs to encrypt a message to you.

sections.title: Finding the Record by Email Address
sections.content:
Email addresses have two parts: the local-part (like "hugh") and the domain (like "example.com"). To make an OPENPGPKEY DNS query, the local-part is first hashed using SHA2-256, truncated to 28 octets, and converted to hexadecimal. The label "_openpgpkey" is added, and the domain is appended.

For example, to fetch the key for hugh@example.com, the DNS query would be for c93f1e400f26708f98cb19d936620da35eec8f72e57f9eec01c1afd6._openpgpkey.example.com. The hashing prevents trivial enumeration of email addresses, though it does not stop determined attackers who can brute-force common names or perform zone walking.

The record can be followed through CNAME and DNAME redirects, provided the key's User IDs include the original email address. Wildcards are allowed only in the local-part ("*@example.com"), so one key can be used for all addresses in a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The email local-part is hashed into a long gibberish string. DNS appends _openpgpkey and the domain, making the full lookup address. This stops simple guessing but not serious attackers.

sections.title: How Mail Servers and Clients Use OPENPGPKEY
sections.content:
When a mail client or server wants to send encrypted email, it performs a DNS lookup for the OPENPGPKEY record. The lookup MUST pass DNSSEC validation, reaching a "Secure" state as specified in RFC 4035. If DNSSEC validation fails, the key MUST NOT be used.

A mail transfer agent (MTA) can use the retrieved key to encrypt the message. It MUST NOT add the key to a permanent keyring beyond the DNS TTL, and it MUST NOT re-encrypt a message that is already encrypted. If the key is revoked, the MTA MUST NOT use it, even if that means sending the message in plaintext.

A mail user agent (MUA) should warn the user if a retrieved OPENPGPKEY key differs from a locally stored key, allowing the user to verify changes. To protect privacy, applications MUST NOT look up the key on every use; they should cache the result for its DNS TTL and avoid revealing which recipients someone is writing to.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending mail, look up the recipient's OPENPGPKEY in DNS, check it is trustworthy using DNSSEC, and encrypt the message with it. Do not save it forever, and tell the user if it changes.

sections.title: Trust and Limitations
sections.content:
OPENPGPKEY is not a replacement for manual fingerprint verification or the OpenPGP web of trust. DNSSEC is only as secure as the DNS administrator's private key. If an attacker steals the DNSSEC key, they can replace any OPENPGPKEY record and read all future messages encrypted with the fake key.

The RFC says that OPENPGPKEY should only be used to encrypt email when the alternative is sending plaintext. It stops passive eavesdropping but not active attacks where someone publishes a fake key. Organizations that require employees' keys to be encrypted and readable by the company should publish the company's escrow key as the OPENPGPKEY record.

DNS queries leak which recipients a user is sending email to, even with DNSSEC. Mail systems should use DNS over TLS and DNS query name minimization to reduce this leakage, and applications should avoid repeated lookups that reveal writing patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC can be broken if its private key is stolen. Encrypted mail using OPENPGPKEY is safer than plaintext but less safe than keys you verify yourself. DNS queries can reveal who you are writing to.

sections.title: Experimental Status
sections.content:
RFC 7929 is Experimental. The goal is to see whether automatically discovering OpenPGP keys increases encrypted email use and whether OPENPGPKEY records scale in large email deployments. Key concerns include the size of records and DNS zones, and whether large email service providers will support the feature.

The specification references RFC 4255 (SSHFP for SSH keys) and RFC 4398 (CERT records for certificates) as prior work, but notes that CERT failed partly due to subtyping, which is now considered bad DNS design. The IETF encourages implementations and deployments to document their experiences so that future standards-track work can benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experiment to see if people will use encrypted email if finding keys is automatic. The IETF wants to learn from real deployments before deciding if this should become an official standard.
